did_you_know.text: The word "mo’ed" is connected with the idea of an appointed time. The festivals are therefore presented not merely as holidays, but as set times with religious meaning.
Shabbat creates a seven-day cycle that does not depend on the moon or the seasons. It is one of the most distinctive features of the biblical calendar.

The phrase "between the evenings" refers to a time late in the day, but Jewish commentators differed about its exact meaning. This disagreement was also connected with the timing of the Passover offering.
Matzah is dough that was not allowed to rise. The prohibition of leaven during Passover turned this simple bread into a symbol of the Exodus and its urgency.
The word "omer" can refer both to a sheaf of grain and to a measure of grain. The term therefore links the harvest in the field with the offering brought to the sanctuary.

The phrase "the day after the Sabbath" led to an ancient debate: the sages interpreted it as the day after the first day of Passover, while other groups understood it as the day after the weekly Sabbath.

The grain products mentioned here—bread, roasted grain, and fresh ears—represent different forms and stages of processing grain. The rule emphasizes that the new harvest was not to be eaten before the offering was brought.
The counting of the Omer is a striking commandment that connects two festivals: it begins at Passover and leads to Shavuot after seven weeks.
The two loaves brought on Shavuot are baked with leaven, unlike most grain offerings, in which leaven is forbidden. This highlights the festival’s connection with the fresh wheat harvest.

The laws of gleaning and leaving the edges of the field helped the poor without taking the entire harvest away from its owner. They are an example of social responsibility built into agricultural law.
The word "teru’ah" describes a loud or broken sound, and Jewish tradition associated it with blowing the shofar. The name "Rosh Hashanah" became common in later periods.

Yom Kippur falls on the tenth day of the seventh month, ten days after the month begins. In Jewish tradition, "afflicting oneself" is mainly associated with fasting, along with an atmosphere of self-examination.
This verse defines Yom Kippur as lasting from evening to evening. It reflects the Jewish principle that days and festivals begin at sunset on the previous day.
In Jewish tradition, the four species are the etrog, lulav, myrtle, and willow. They come from different kinds of landscapes and bring together a fruit tree, a palm, a shrub, and a riverside tree.

The sukkah recalls the Israelites’ temporary life in the wilderness, so it is built as a temporary structure rather than a permanent home. Each year, the festival invites people to leave their comfort zone and live simply for a short time.
